newsitem.title: JAPAN: US to act if Japan breaks insurance pact -- official.
newsitem.headline: US to act if Japan breaks insurance pact -- official.

text.p: The United States will take "appropriate action" if Japan does not uphold a 1994 bilateral pact on deregulation on Japan's insurance market, a U.S. official said on Thursday.

The official, speaking after talks on Wednesday in Tokyo on implementation of the 1994 agreement, told reporters that significant gaps remained between the two sides and that Japanese negotiators had withdrawn some compromise proposals made in earlier talks in Vancouver, Canada.
But he also said he believed a negotiated solution could still be achieved, and that the two sides would be in touch about setting dates for further talks.

"Let me just say it is our hope that we can resolve this matter through negotiations...but we have reached an agreement in 1994 and the agreement must be upheld, and if it is not upheld it is necessary to take appropriate action," the official said.

U.S. and Japanese working-level officials met in Tokyo on Wednesday for talks on the insurance dispute, the first discussions since negotiatiors failed to reach agreement by a July 31 deadline at talks in Vancouver.

The dispute centres on U.S. allegations that Japan is reneging on the 1994 pact by moving to open up the so-called "third sector" niche insurance market before substantially deregulating its primary life and non-life sectors.

Asked about the U.S. response should the Finance Ministry allow the non-life subsidiaries of Japanese life insurers to enter the personal accident insurance business, the official said: "Our position is the agreement must be upheld. The agreement says there should be no radical change in the business environment of the third sector until the primary sector has been deregulated."
"There has not been deregulation in the primary sector, therefore there should not be radical change in the third sector."
The Finance Ministry is expected to decide conditions for granting licences to life insurers' non-life subsidiaries by October 1.

"In its action on October 1, the Japanese government should not take action which prejudices the negotiations, which invalidates the U.S. position or unilaterally adopts the Japanese position," the official said.

He also said the Japanese government had a "positive attitude" towards the negotiations, and that he thought a negotiated solution was possible. "I am not here to foretell doom and gloom on October 1, because I think it is quite possible to find a solution."

The official also said both sides hoped Finance Minister Wataru Kubo would be able to meet U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky in Washington. Kubo is expected to go to Washington for meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank starting on September 24, but his schedule is not yet finalised.
The official also said the U.S. expressed concern that the Japanese withdrawal of earlier compromise proposals would make it more difficult to reach an agreement.
